note: Wren Phonics reading-practice guide (b409, 2026-10-08). Own words throughout. provenance: Wren original, b409, 2026-10-08.
overview: Alongside the daily phonics lesson, every child reads their matched decodable book in small reading-practice sessions, three times a week, re-reading the same book across the week rather than moving to a new one each time. Re-reading is deliberate: the first read is hard work (decoding), and only repetition frees up attention for expression and understanding — repeated reading of a matched decodable book like this is common practice across systematic synthetic phonics teaching, set out here in Wren's own words as three sessions: Sound it out, Read it with feeling, and Talk about it.
whyRereading: A child meeting a decodable book for the first time is spending almost all their attention on decoding individual words. Reading the identical book again lets known words become faster and freer, so the same three reads move from "hard decoding work" to "fluent, expressive reading" without ever asking the child to read anything un-matched to their taught code.
grouping: Group by current phase/week position, not by age or room — a child's key worker or teacher should know which week's book each child is matched to from the programme's own week-by-week plan.

Small groups of 2-4 children reading the same book work well for sessions 1 and 2; session 3 (Talk about it) can run 1:1, in pairs, or as a slightly larger group discussion since no one is decoding aloud for the whole group at once.
A child who joins mid-term is matched to a book by their placement assessment, not by their year group's current week.
Keep a session short — 10-15 minutes is normal for a small group at Reception; sessions can run a little longer by Year 1 as stamina grows, but a tired, rushed re-read helps no one.

sessions.name: Sound it out
sessions.how: Introduce the book: show the cover, say the title, and run through the session card's "Sounds to practise" and any tricky words or pre-teach vocabulary before anyone opens the book — a brief warm-up, not a lesson. Then each child reads the whole book aloud (round-robin by page in a small group, or independently with the adult listening in), decoding every word rather than being told it or guessing from the picture. Support a stuck word by prompting sound-by-sound, not by supplying the word.
sessions.afterwards: Note anything that needed heavy support — that is what the next same-day boost slot in the daily lesson should target, not a reason to hold the book back.

sessions.name: Read it with feeling
sessions.how: Same book, second read. Decoding should already be lighter, so attention shifts to how it sounds: pace, pausing at punctuation, and the specific expression line given on that book's session card (a quoted line and how to read it). Model it once yourself, then have each child try that one line, and read the rest of the book through as normal.
sessions.afterwards: This is a fluency signal, not a performance to mark — a flat, word-by-word read on session 2 usually means decoding is still the bottleneck; go back to session 1's support rather than drilling expression in isolation.

sessions.name: Talk about it
sessions.how: Third read (or, for a very small group short on time, skip straight to discussion after one more listen) followed by the book's own comprehension questions — a mix of retrieval (what happened), inference (why/how, using clues in the text and pictures) and vocabulary (what a word means). The adult asks the questions aloud; a child never needs to decode the question itself, only answer from the story.
sessions.afterwards: Record what you noticed on the separate group reading record — not every answer to every question, just anything that tells you whether to move this group on to the next matched book or keep practising this one.

timetabling: A simple weekly shape: Sound it out early in the week (e.g. Monday/Tuesday), Read it with feeling mid-week (Wednesday), Talk about it later (Thursday/Friday) — so each session has had a day or two since the last to let the previous read settle.
Run reading-practice sessions alongside, not instead of, the whole-class daily phonics lesson — the lesson teaches the code; reading practice applies it to a real, matched book in a small group.
A rolling timetable across the week lets one adult see 3-4 small groups for 10-15 minutes each, which comfortably covers a class across the week without needing extra staffing.
When a new matched book becomes available partway through a week, finish the current book's three sessions before starting the new one — three full sessions matter more than switching promptly.
